title: Japan holds at 1.25% and more than doubles planned ETF sales
summary: The Bank of Japan made two decisions with different implementation dates on October 30. By eight votes to one it kept the uncollateralized overnight call-rate guideline near 1.25%. By a unanimous vote it approved a faster pace of sales from its exchange-traded fund portfolio, starting in January 2027. The Bank also published a new judgment that underlying inflation was broadly consistent with its 2% target. An analyst using only an overnight rate chart would see a flat observation on a day when the Board changed both its assessment of price stability and the prospective supply of equity funds to the market (statement, sections 1–2, and October Outlook, summary).

The annual ETF sales pace rose from approximately ¥330 billion to ¥860 billion at book value, around 2.6 times the previous amount. At the market-to-book ratio of ETFs sold in January–September 2026, the new amount would be worth roughly ¥2.46 trillion at market prices. The Bank calibrated it to around 0.1% of trading value, using Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market turnover over that period. Its previous plan had been benchmarked to the scale of an earlier programme of sales of stocks bought from financial institutions, around 0.05% of turnover at the time. Changes in market turnover and valuation explain why a roughly doubled target share of trading does not translate into precisely double the book-value amount (section 2 and footnote 1).

The Bank said sales since January had proceeded smoothly while equity turnover expanded. The reference sheet illustrates the scale of the remaining portfolio. Dividing end-September holdings at book value by the annual pace produces around 43 years under the new plan versus 112 under the previous one. These are static illustrations, not promised completion dates. Sales would be distributed broadly in proportion to individual funds’ share of the holdings and spread across time. The Bank could adjust or temporarily suspend sales as market conditions changed within its annual approach. Planned J-REIT sales stayed near ¥5 billion per year at book value. A projection that accelerated both ETF and real-estate disposals would misstate the decision (statement, footnotes 2–4, and accompanying ETF sales reference).

Changes in the inflation outlook mattered independently. The Bank judged that rising wages and prices were already reinforcing one another and that medium- to long-term inflation expectations were around 2%. Its median forecast for CPI excluding fresh food in fiscal 2027 rose from 2.4% in July to 2.6%, while fiscal 2026 stayed at 2.5% and fiscal 2028 at 2.0%. The projections excluded the proposed reduction in consumption tax on food and beverages. Higher energy and semiconductor costs and earlier yen depreciation could temporarily take observed inflation above the underlying pace. The majority assessed price risks as tilted upward and growth risks as broadly balanced. Underlying inflation at target describes the Bank’s current assessment. It does not require every observable price index or every forecast year to register exactly 2% (October Outlook, summary and forecast appendix).

Hajime Takata proposed raising the overnight guideline to 1.5%. His reasoning centred on the speed of adjustment toward a neutral interest rate now that he judged underlying inflation at target. The majority also recognized a change in the inflation regime and continued to envisage further tightening, yet it did not endorse another immediate increase following September’s move. The dissent gave a direction and magnitude for a different October decision. It gave no numerical estimate of the neutral rate or schedule for reaching it. Treating it as a Board forecast for the next meeting would exaggerate the agreement among members (statement, voting note, and October Outlook, section IV).

The rate decision, the ETF change and the Bank’s View were public at 12:02 Japan time. An intraday movement in an equity benchmark could reflect expected discount rates, changes in expected official ETF supply or revised earnings prospects. The January 2027 implementation date gives researchers a separate opportunity to examine realized sales and liquidity, starting from what had already been anticipated after the October release. The announcement itself does not establish that accelerated selling depressed Japanese stocks. Its market impact depends on expectations, liquidity and the distribution of exposure across funds and constituent shares (statement, release reference and ETF sales reference).

questions.question: Did the ETF announcement create a measurable price effect beyond rate expectations?
questions.detail: Compare returns in highly versus lightly represented equities, controlling for sector, market beta and market capitalization. Check ETF prices relative to underlying holdings where synchronized quotes are available. Include the simultaneous changes in swap rates and the yen. A broad equity move with little cross-sectional relation to ETF exposure would weaken a direct sales-supply interpretation.

questions.question: How material is the planned sales flow under different liquidity and valuation conditions?
questions.detail: Translate the ¥860 billion annual book-value pace into market value under several market-to-book ratios. Scale it by contemporaneous turnover across individual funds and volatile trading sessions. A modest share of annual aggregate turnover can correspond to a larger fraction in a smaller fund, especially if turnover falls or sales are temporarily interrupted.

questions.question: Did recognition that underlying inflation had reached target change the expected terminal rate?
questions.detail: Compare changes at the next few meetings with longer yen forwards around 12:02, while monitoring foreign yields and price-based inflation compensation. Use the October forecast vintage, which excluded the proposed tax cut. A front-loaded rate change and a persistent increase in distant forwards have different implications for the market’s neutral-rate assessment.
